1135.title: Shaving or trimming
1135.hook: men shave or trim, women cut a fingertip's length
1135.howItsDone: After the stoning and the sacrifice, male pilgrims shave their heads or trim their hair and women cut a small length from the ends, which releases them from most of the restrictions of ihram.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the sacrifice, its meat eaten and shared, and only the devotion reaching God. Your line: shared meat.

"And those who trim?" It's the companions asking. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ has just asked God to have mercy on those who shave their heads. Some of the men listening have only trimmed theirs. So they ask: and those who trim? He repeats the prayer for those who shave. They ask again. Only after asking more than once do they hear him include them: and those who trim. A small, almost funny exchange, people making sure they're counted. Today, shaving or trimming.
screen: `MERCY ON THOSE WHO SHAVE.` → `AND THOSE WHO TRIM?` → `AND THOSE WHO TRIM.`

segments.voice: Start with why hair matters here at all. In ihram, pilgrims don't cut their hair; Surah Al-Baqarah tells them not to shave their heads until the offering has reached its place. Then, after the stoning and the sacrifice, it's cut. Anas reports in Sahih Muslim that the Prophet came back to his place at Mina, called the barber, pointed to one side of his head and then the other, and gave his hair away to the people. Second, the two ways. The hadith from the hook, in Sahih al-Bukhari, praises those who shave, and when asked, includes those who trim. Both are allowed for men. Shaving is the fuller act; trimming is enough. Third, women. A report from Ibn Abbas in Sunan Abi Dawud says women don't shave; they only shorten. Jurists describe it as cutting about a fingertip's length from the ends. Fourth, what the cut does. It marks a release. Much of what ihram held back is lifted, and the pilgrim can wear ordinary clothes again. Surah Al-Fath pictures believers entering the Sacred Mosque in safety, heads shaved and hair cut, without fear. One more thing. On that busy day people did the rites in a jumble, and came to the Prophet worried. One said he'd shaved before sacrificing. The answer, in Bukhari: do it, there's no harm. The schools of law later discussed when a change of order needs making up. But that day, the worried were met with ease. So the end of ihram is something anyone can see: a shaved head, or hair a little shorter at the ends.

segments.voice: Turn your hands over and look at your nails, growing all this time without any help from you, the way a pilgrim's hair grows through ihram. Let them stand for the stretch you've just come through, this week, this season, and ask whether something in it is finished. If you pray, say a quiet bismillah for what comes next; if not, just breathe.
Shaving or trimming. Men shave or trim their hair, and women cut a little from the ends, marking the release from ihram. Today's word.
Your line: a new start. Something ends, so something else can begin clean. I'll be here tomorrow.

1136.title: The tawaf of Ifadah
1136.howItsDone: After the stoning, sacrifice and haircut, pilgrims go to Mecca and circle the Ka'ba in the tawaf of Ifadah, a required pillar of Hajj, often followed by the walk between Safa and Marwa.

segments.voice: Yesterday: shaving or trimming, the haircut that marks a release from ihram. Your line: a new start.

The Hajj is nearly over, and the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ is told that Safiyyah, one of his wives, has started her period. His first question is practical: is she going to hold us up? Will the whole party have to wait for her? Then a second question. Did she already do the tawaf, the circling of the Ka'ba, after the day of sacrifice? Yes, they tell him, she did. Then, he says, let's go. One question decided whether everyone waited. Today, the tawaf of Ifadah.
screen: `IS SHE GOING TO HOLD US UP?` → `DID SHE ALREADY CIRCLE?` → `THEN LET'S GO.`

segments.voice: First, where it falls. The pilgrims have stood at Arafah, slept at Muzdalifah, thrown the stones, offered the sacrifice and cut their hair. Then they go up to Mecca. Jabir's account in Sahih Muslim says the Prophet rode to the House, circled it, and prayed zuhr in Mecca. Then he came to his own clan as they drew water from Zamzam, and drank. Second, the Qur'an's line for it. In Surah Al-Hajj, after the sacrifice, pilgrims are told to finish their unkempt state, fulfill their vows, and "go around the ancient House." Commentators connect that line to this circling. Third, why it's called essential. Tradition counts it among the pillars of Hajj, the parts without which the Hajj isn't complete. Some other rites, if missed, can be made up with an offering. This one has to be done. That's the weight behind Safiyyah's story: his question suggests the whole party would have waited for it, and once he heard it was done, nothing else stood in the way. Fourth, what it finishes. With this circling, and the walk between Safa and Marwa for those who still owe it, the last restrictions of ihram lift. The pilgrim who arrived at the boundary in two white cloths is now, in the eyes of the law, free. One more circling comes at the very end, but that belongs to a later day. Today's is the one the Hajj stands on. After all the big, open places, the plain, the valley, the pillars, the journey comes back to the same small center it started from, and goes around it again.
screen: `UP TO MECCA, AFTER THE SACRIFICE.` · `GO AROUND THE ANCIENT HOUSE.` · `A PILLAR OF HAJJ.` · `THE LAST OF IHRAM LIFTS.` · then, large: `THEN LET'S GO.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind something you've nearly finished: a letter that only needs signing, a repair that needs one more screw. Find the last step, the one the whole thing stands on, and see yourself doing it slowly, all the way to the end. If you pray, ask for help finishing it; if not, let the finished version rest in your mind.
The tawaf of Ifadah. The circling of the Ka'ba after Arafah and the day of sacrifice, a pillar of Hajj that has to be done. Today's word.
Your line: the essential circling. Some steps can be made up; this one carries the rest. Go gently.

1137.title: The days of tashriq
1137.hook: days of eating, drinking and remembrance in Mina (Muslim)
1137.howItsDone: In the days after Eid al-Adha, pilgrims stay in Mina, stone the pillars each afternoon, eat and drink, and say the takbir, and these days are not fasted.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the tawaf of Ifadah, the circling the Hajj stands on. Your line: the essential circling.

When the pilgrimage was over, in the days before Islam, people would gather and talk about their fathers: whose ancestor fed the most guests, whose clan had the proudest name. That's the scene commentators on the Qur'an give for a verse in Surah Al-Baqarah: when the rites are done, remember God as you used to remember your fathers, or with a stronger remembrance. Same gathering, same tents, same food. A different name on everyone's lips. Today, the days of tashriq.
screen: `TALK OF FATHERS.` → `REMEMBER GOD AS YOU REMEMBERED THEM.` → `OR MORE.`

segments.voice: After the day of sacrifice, the pilgrims go back down to Mina and stay. These are the days of tashriq. First, what they're for. In Sahih Muslim, the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ says the days of tashriq are days of eating and drinking, and in one wording, of remembering God. You met that saying back on day five hundred fourteen, at Eid. Not fasting days, scholars conclude. Feast days. Food is part of the worship here, not a break from it. Second, the counted days. Surah Al-Baqarah tells the pilgrims to remember God through the appointed days, then offers a choice: whoever hurries off after two days, no sin on him, and whoever stays on, no sin on him either, for the one who is mindful of God. Two good ways out; the condition the verse names is mindfulness, not the schedule. Third, the stones again. Aisha describes, in Sunan Abi Dawud, how the Prophet stayed at Mina those nights and stoned the pillars each day after noon, a takbir with each pebble. At the first two pillars, she says, he stood a long time in du'a. At the last, he didn't stop. So the days hold a rhythm: a meal, a walk to the pillars, a long stand, a meal again. Fourth, how a meal remembers. The young Umar ibn Abi Salamah once ate with the Prophet, his hand wandering all over the dish. He was told: say God's name, eat with your right hand, and eat from what's in front of you. Three small things, and a whole way of eating. In Mina the feast and the remembrance aren't separate. Someone passes the bread, and says bismillah as they take it.

segments.voice: Take something small, a date or a glass of water, or picture your next meal. If you pray, say bismillah before the first bite and alhamdulillah after; if not, pause and think of everyone it took to bring it to you. Then eat slowly, with your right hand, from what's in front of you.
The days of tashriq. The days after the sacrifice, spent in Mina: days of eating, drinking, stoning the pillars and remembering God. Today's word.
Your line: eat and remember. At Mina, a meal is one more way of remembering. See you for the farewell.

1138.title: The farewell tawaf
1138.hook: a last circling before leaving Mecca
1138.howItsDone: Before leaving Mecca, pilgrims circle the Ka'ba one last time in the farewell tawaf; women on their period are excused from it, and the schools differ on whether it is required or strongly recommended.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the days of tashriq, days of eating, drinking and remembering God at Mina. Your line: eat and remember.

People are already leaving. The rites are done, the days at Mina are over, and pilgrims are heading off in every direction, home to wherever home is. Ibn Abbas remembers the moment. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ stops them with a sentence: none of you should leave until the last thing you do is at the House. Not the last purchase, not the last meal. The House. So before the road home, there's one more walk around the Ka'ba. Today, the farewell tawaf.
screen: `LEAVING IN EVERY DIRECTION.` → `NONE OF YOU SHOULD LEAVE…` → `…UNTIL THE LAST THING IS THE HOUSE.`

segments.voice: First, the rule. Ibn Abbas's report, in Sahih Muslim, is simple: let the last of your time be at the House. A pilgrim's stay ends where it began, circling the Ka'ba. Second, the exception. In another report from Ibn Abbas, in Sahih al-Bukhari, people were commanded to make their last act at the House, except that it was lightened for a woman on her period. She may set out without it. Two days ago, Safiyyah's story showed which circling couldn't be skipped. This is the one that could be lifted. Third, how the schools weigh it. Some schools of law hold the farewell tawaf to be required of pilgrims leaving Mecca, so that missing it calls for an offering. Others hold it to be strongly recommended. Each school reads the same reports, and each has its reasons. Fourth, the word itself. Wada' means a farewell. Tradition calls the Prophet's own pilgrimage, the one these lessons have been following, the Farewell Pilgrimage, Hajjat al-Wada', and he did not make another. You met that pilgrimage back on day two hundred eighty-four. So two goodbyes fold together here: a pilgrim's goodbye to the House, and the memory of the Prophet's goodbye to his people. What the rite teaches is a way of leaving. Not slipping out the side door. Not letting the last memory be a crowded shop or a line for the bus. Going back to the center once more, and leaving from there, with the place you're leaving as the last thing you saw.
screen: `LET THE LAST OF IT BE AT THE HOUSE.` · `LIGHTENED FOR A WOMAN ON HER PERIOD.` · `REQUIRED, OR STRONGLY RECOMMENDED.` · `WADA': A FAREWELL.` · then, large: `GOODBYE TO THE HOUSE.`

segments.voice: Think of a goodbye that's coming, the end of a job, a friend moving, a visit with a parent that ends on Sunday, or one you rushed in a parking lot or a text. Picture how you'd want that last moment to go, who you'd look at and what you'd say. If you pray, hold that person in your du'a; if not, simply hold them in mind.
The farewell tawaf. The last circling of the Ka'ba before a pilgrim leaves Mecca, so the final act of the journey is at the House. Today's word.
Your line: goodbye to the house. The way you leave is part of the visit. Go well.

1139.title: Visiting Medina
1139.hook: many visit the Prophet's Mosque, though it isn't part of Hajj
1139.howItsDone: Some pilgrims travel to Medina before or after Hajj to pray in the Prophet's Mosque and greet him at his grave; Muslims send salawat on him in prayer and when his name is mentioned.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the farewell tawaf, the last circling before leaving Mecca. Your line: goodbye to the house.

Don't saddle up for a journey, the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ said, except to three mosques. That's how a report in Sahih al-Bukhari puts it: the Sacred Mosque in Mecca, the Messenger's own mosque in Medina, and the Aqsa Mosque in Jerusalem. The Hajj is over, its rites finished in Mecca. But some pilgrims, before the pilgrimage or after it, take the road north to the city where he lived, prayed and is buried. Today, visiting Medina.
screen: `ONLY THREE MOSQUES.` → `THE MESSENGER'S MOSQUE.` → `THE ROAD NORTH.`

segments.voice: First, what it isn't. Visiting Medina isn't part of Hajj. A pilgrim who goes straight home from Mecca has a complete Hajj. The visit is its own act, often joined to the trip because the road is already long. Second, the mosque. In another report in Bukhari, the Prophet says a prayer in this mosque of his is better than a thousand prayers elsewhere, except the Sacred Mosque. And he says that between his house and his pulpit is a garden from the gardens of Paradise. Visitors try to pray in that small stretch, the Rawdah, the garden. Third, the greeting. His grave is there, in what was once Aisha's room. Visitors stand near it and say, as-salamu alayka ya rasul Allah: peace be on you, messenger of God. In Sunan Abi Dawud, the Prophet says that no one greets him but that God returns his soul to him so that he returns the greeting. Scholars have discussed how to frame the journey. Some say the traveler should set out for the mosque, and greet the Prophet once there, holding to the report about three mosques. Others hold the visit to the grave itself to be a recommended act. Both send peace on him. Fourth, the line under all of it. Surah Al-Ahzab says: "Lo! Allah and His angels shower blessings on the Prophet. O ye who believe! Ask blessings on him and salute him with a worthy salutation." Muslims call that sending salawat, and it isn't tied to Medina. It can be said anywhere, in a kitchen, on a bus, inside the daily prayer. The visitors say it a few steps from him; everyone else, from wherever they are.
screen: `NOT PART OF HAJJ.` · `A GARDEN BETWEEN HOUSE AND PULPIT.` · `HE RETURNS THE GREETING.` · `SEND BLESSINGS FROM ANYWHERE.` · then, large: `PEACE BE ON YOU, MESSENGER OF GOD.`

segments.voice: If you pray, say slowly, as-salamu alayka ayyuha an-nabiyy, peace be on you, O Prophet, the words from the tashahhud in the prayer, or sallallahu alayhi wa sallam, a few times, unhurried. If you don't, think of a teacher whose words still reach you, and send them, in your mind, a plain thank you.

1140.title: The Hajj of the heart
1140.hook: those who can't go share in it by fasting Arafah and by longing
1140.howItsDone: Muslims who cannot make the pilgrimage may fast on the day of Arafah, say the takbir through the first days of Dhul Hijjah, offer a sacrifice at Eid al-Adha if able, and ask God for the chance to go.

segments.voice: Yesterday: visiting Medina, and peace sent on the Prophet from near or far. Your line: peace on you, messenger.

They came asking for something to ride. An expedition was setting out, and these men wanted to go, but they had no mount and no money for one. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ told them he had nothing to carry them on. Surah At-Tawbah keeps what happened next. They turned away, their eyes overflowing with tears, grieving that they couldn't find the means. The Qur'an says there is no blame on them. They stayed home. Their tears went on the record anyway. Today, the Hajj of the heart.
screen: `NOTHING TO RIDE.` → `EYES OVERFLOWING.` → `NO BLAME ON THEM.`

segments.voice: This path began the pilgrimage with a condition: the Hajj is due on those who can find a way. Today is for everyone else. First, the men in tears. The verse doesn't scold them for staying home. It names their grief and lifts the blame. Wanting to go and being unable is different from not wanting to go. Second, the people left behind. Anas reports, in Sahih al-Bukhari, that on the way home from that expedition the Prophet told his companions: there are people in Medina who were with you on every road you traveled and every valley you crossed. They were held back by an excuse. Held back, and still with you. Third, a rule of thumb from the same collection. When a servant of God falls ill or travels, the Prophet said, the good he used to do while healthy and at home is still written for him. The record follows habit and intention, not just location. Fourth, what people at home actually do. On the day of Arafah, while the pilgrims stand on the plain, Muslims who aren't there are encouraged to fast, and Sahih Muslim records the Prophet's praise for that fast. And in the first days of Dhul Hijjah, a person who plans to offer a sacrifice is told, in another report in Muslim, to leave their hair and nails uncut until it's done, a small echo of the pilgrim's restraint, kept at home, far from Mecca. So while the plain fills, someone in an ordinary kitchen keeps the fast: their share of the day.

1141.title: Five pillars, one house
1141.hook: the pillars hold up a life the way the prayer hall's columns hold the roof
1141.howItsDone: Muslims learn the five pillars, the testimony, prayer, zakat, the fast of Ramadan and the Hajj, from the report of Ibn Umar, and some teachers present them as the supports of one building.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the Hajj of the heart, taking part from home through longing and intention. Your line: longing counts.

A prayer hall has a carpet, light from the windows, a niche that points toward Mecca. And it has columns. They stand row after row, doing their one job, and the roof stays up. A column is easy to overlook until it's missing. That's the picture behind a report the Prophet's companions passed on, one that turns religion into architecture. You met it back on day nine. Today, the five pillars, and the house they hold up.
screen: `EASY TO OVERLOOK.` → `ROW AFTER ROW, ONE JOB.` → `RELIGION AS ARCHITECTURE.`

segments.voice: First, the report. Abdullah ibn Umar relates, in Sahih Muslim, that the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ said: Islam is built upon five. Testifying that there is no god but God and that Muhammad is His messenger. Establishing the prayer. Giving zakat. Fasting Ramadan. And the Hajj. Notice the verb. Not ruled by five, not summed up in five. Built. Islam is described as a building. Second, how carefully it was kept. In the same collection, a man repeats the list back to Ibn Umar and puts the Hajj before the fast. Ibn Umar stops him: no, fasting Ramadan and then the Hajj; that is how I heard it from the Messenger of God. A small correction, and it shows how closely he held to the exact words. Third, look back. This block walked through the building one pillar at a time. The testimony, two sentences. The prayer, its times and its stillness. Zakat, the share that purifies. The fast, its shield and its two joys. And these last weeks, the pilgrimage: the boundary and the two white cloths, Arafah and Muzdalifah, the stones, the sacrifice, the haircut, the circlings, the farewell, Medina, and the longing of those who stay home. Fourth, why one house and not five separate rules. The pillars hold the same roof, and they bend to the person under it. Zakat falls on those with wealth, the fast has its exemptions, the Hajj is due only on those who are able. The building is drawn to fit the people who live in it. One house, five columns, and a roof over a whole life.

segments.voice: Go through the pillars slowly, the way you'd walk past columns in a hall: the testimony, the prayer, giving, the fast, the pilgrimage or the longing for it, and rest your attention on the one you're strongest in. If you're learning about Islam rather than practicing it, ask which of your own daily supports is steadiest; if you pray, thank God for what's holding. The weak one can wait for tomorrow.
